analysis.one_liner: Bans paraquat, organophosphate, and neonicotinoid pesticides and tightens EPA pesticide review.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or any action in the Senate Agriculture Committee, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban by law three groups of pesticides linked to serious health harms — organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat — and bar the continued sale of banned stocks. It would also automatically suspend any pesticide the European Union or Canada has banned, force EPA to finish its reviews of dangerous pesticides on a 15-year clock, cap emergency exemptions, require disclosure of secret inert ingredients, let local communities set stricter pesticide rules, and create mandatory reporting of farmworker poisonings with penalties for employers who retaliate against workers who report [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Children, farmworkers (who are disproportionately exposed to pesticides and are often migrant or seasonal workers), rural communities near treated fields, consumers, and pollinators and wildlife would gain if the bill passed. Farmworkers would get mandatory incident reporting, $25,000 rewards for reporting employers who cover up poisonings, protection from retaliation and immigration enforcement tied to reports, bilingual labels, and whistleblower-style job protection [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Immediately cancels the registrations of all organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, and revokes the legal tolerance levels that allow their residues in food [S2] [S3].

Requires EPA to automatically suspend any pesticide registered in the US that the European Union or Canada has banned, with cancellation within two years unless the EPA finds the foreign ban clearly erroneous [S2] [S3].

Requires employers to report farmworker poisonings to the EPA through an online system with anonymous reporting, with fines of $1,000 per day for failing to report, criminal penalties for pressuring workers not to report, a $25,000 reward for reports that expose unreported incidents, and a ban on immigration enforcement based on a report [S3].
Requires pesticide labels to list all inert ingredients, which the bill notes can make up 99 percent of a product and can include carcinogenic and toxic chemicals [S2] [S3].
Lets cities, counties, and other local governments enact their own pesticide protections, which states currently preempt [S3].

Puts a 15-year clock on EPA pesticide reviews, suspends pesticides whose reviews are overdue, ends the sale of existing stocks of suspended or canceled pesticides, limits emergency exemptions to no more than two years per product per location in any ten-year period, and requires conditional registrations to be completed within two years [S2] [S3].
Protects employees who participate in pesticide proceedings from being fired or otherwise punished, with reinstatement, back pay, and damages available through the Labor Department [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers would lose the legal sales of major product lines — paraquat (Syngenta's flagship herbicide), neonicotinoids (Bayer, Syngenta, Corteva), and the organophosphate class. Farms that rely on those chemicals would have to switch products or practices, and the bill's sponsors' findings say billions of pounds are applied each year, so the transition would affect a large share of US agriculture [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and farms that use them

drawbacks.text: The bans take effect by operation of law, with no further proceedings, even where EPA's own scientific review of a chemical is underway — the bill declares entire pesticide classes to 'generally cause unreasonable adverse effects' by statute rather than by individual EPA determination [S3].

When reviewing foreign bans, EPA is barred from considering any economic analysis of the costs or benefits of continuing to register the pesticide, which removes the usual cost-benefit check from the decision [S3].

Farmers would lose currently legal tools on short notice, and for some crops and pests there may not be ready substitutes; the costs of switching would fall on farms and potentially on food prices, and the bill includes no transition assistance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong and documented in the bill's own findings: scientists have repeatedly linked organophosphates to neurodevelopmental harm in children, paraquat greatly raises Parkinson's risk and can cause organ failure, and federal wildlife agencies found organophosphates jeopardize 97 percent of endangered species [S2]. The main honest objections are procedural and economic: canceling whole classes by statute overrides EPA's individualized science review, foreign bans become presumptively binding, and farms would absorb the adjustment cost with no transition help. For farmworkers and children the benefits are direct; for growers the burden is real but bounded to three chemical classes plus stricter review rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never held a hearing or acted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by Sens. Gillibrand, Sanders, Warren, and Schatz as original cosponsors [S3] [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5] [S1].
The bill had 5 cosponsors: 4 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers are better off: paraquat, neonicotinoids, and organophosphates remain fully legal to sell and use in the US, and the other changes — automatic suspension of EU-banned pesticides, a 15-year review clock, inert-ingredient disclosure, and mandatory farmworker poisoning reports — never happened either. Farmworkers, children, and communities near treated fields gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Gillibrand, Sanders, Warren, and Schatz
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; Sanders is the Independent.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Agrochemical industry groups and farm organizations
against.role: Pesticide manufacturers and agricultural trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed prior versions of this bill and lobbied against banning paraquat, neonicotinoids, and organophosphates, which are among their largest-selling products.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-led Agriculture Committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: Paraquat, neonicotinoids, and organophosphates would be banned outright with no sale of existing stocks, and residues in food would lose their legal tolerances. The industry profits from products the bill's findings link to child neurodevelopmental harm, Parkinson's disease, and pollinator collapse, so its interest ran against the health protections [S2] [S3].

Growers would lose legal tools on short notice and bear the cost of switching, though the ban of emergency-exemption workarounds and overdue EPA reviews would eventually give them more certain, up-to-date safety decisions [S3].
Stricter rules and faster suspension of banned pesticides reduce pesticide drift and keep cheaper-to-them competitors from using chemicals banned abroad [S3].
